source_title: Professor Jiang's Interview with Russia Today @PredictiveHistory

interactions.summary: The host frames the interview around whether history can still be protected from geopolitical manipulation after the twentieth century and the rhetoric of the 'right side of history.'
Jiang gives a brief courtesy acceptance before the substantive questioning begins.
The host summarizes psychohistory as applying psychoanalysis to geopolitics and asks why entrenched power holders would ever let a wiser predictive understanding of social behavior benefit humanity.

Jiang defines psychohistory as psychoanalysis joined to game theory, models nation-states as persons with memory and motive, argues empathy and historical behavior make prediction possible, and says elite hubris eventually collapses societies so later elites can rebuild on better historical standards.

The host argues that serious history requires a non-narcissistic reading of past human dynamics, then asks how Jiang navigates Western claims to stand on the 'right side of history' when those claims also intimidate dissenters.

Jiang replies that history is usually taught as indoctrination rather than objective inquiry, treats Fukuyama-style end-of-history liberal triumphalism as propaganda, and says neoliberal history-writing serves colonial exploitation, inequality, corruption, and war.
Jiang closes the prior answer by saying history can only be rescued from indoctrination when it is forced to produce predictions that can fail.

The host argues that serious history should judge what is possible for a specific society at a specific moment rather than imposing abstract universal goods, then asks why modern geopolitics lacks that ordinary realism.

Jiang answers that elite moral language is usually a power instrument, that Western values are not universally suited to human life, and that prediction disciplines moral prejudice by forcing actors to face limits.
The host pushes back against binary moral schemes by using Shanghai as an example of a society that combines collective discipline with vivid individual expression.
Jiang agrees that societies are plural and dynamic and says prosperity depends on recognizing diversity, openness, and the spectrum of viewpoints within human communities.
The host asks whether game theory is actually used in geopolitics and whether current disorder reflects a deliberate strategy or the absence of one.

Jiang says applied game theory fails when it becomes mathematical without empathy, argues American hegemony treats its own choices as rational and everyone else's as irrational, and uses Ukraine to claim that Russia's war becomes legible only when one models NATO expansion from Russia's position.
The host pauses the Ukraine thread to ask what Trump represents as a political phenomenon inside a disintegrating American-led order.

Jiang compares Trump to Julius Caesar, arguing he appears when a corrupt oligarchic republic can no longer reconcile elites and people and therefore starts longing for a warrior-savior, a process Jiang says could ignite American civil war.
The host asks how different states are adjusting to a Trumpian America and where that adaptive behavior suggests the world is heading.

Jiang says Trump has stripped away the liberal facade of American empire and revealed open bullying, piracy, and Monroe-Doctrine coercion, which forces each power bloc to respond according to its own position inside the imperial order.
The host notes that the new American security language sounds less universalist about democracy and asks whether that could mean reduced interventionism, at least outside the Western Hemisphere.

Jiang rejects the idea of retreat, arguing that America is only shifting from liberal hypocrisy to a classic divide-and-rule strategy in which allied vassals and proxies absorb the fighting against rivals such as China and Russia.
After the break, the host recalls Jiang's 2024 warning about a second Trump presidency leading toward war with Iran and asks whether another American attack is likely in the coming year.

Jiang says another attack on Iran is both likely and near because the American empire fears a peaceful Russia-Iran-China Eurasian bloc that could bypass American sea power, so Washington will eventually try to destroy Iran to block that integration.

The host distinguishes decisive victory from limited but damaging sabotage and asks whether Iran can protect itself against the kind of strikes that wreck development without producing a clean American conquest.

Jiang agrees that America is not seeking classical conquest but infrastructure sabotage, argues Iran has little practical way to stop that despite its defenses, then predicts that American overstretch will collapse U.S. power and leave Israel as the new regional superpower inheriting its Middle East assets.
The host applies Jiang's own war-winning criteria to Ukraine and asks which side is actually winning.

Jiang says Russia already won the war over a year ago, reads the current slow pace as a deliberate effort to preserve civilians and infrastructure for postwar rule, and predicts that European refusal to accept defeat will prolong the conflict through outside reinforcement rather than reverse the outcome.
The host reuses Jiang's sunk-cost-fallacy analogy for Ukraine and asks who, if anyone, will force the gamblers away from the table, specifically pressing for whether that break could happen in 2026.

Jiang answers that the Ukrainian, European, and American elites all profit from prolonging the war, so there is no internal actor with an incentive to stop it; instead the conflict functions as a Western military-industrial cash extraction scheme.
The host recalls Jiang's Odessa forecast and asks whether a landlocked Ukraine after losing the city could still survive as a sovereign or semi-independent state.

Jiang reframes the conflict as a Europe-backed war on Russia, says Odessa is the final stand because Ukraine becomes a dependent rump state if it falls, and predicts Europe will answer by drafting men into Odessa, producing domestic upheaval, regime change, and eventually a ceasefire with Russia.
The host tests Jiang's optimism about a European peace settlement by raising the darker possibility that Europe could escalate toward a broader global war instead of cutting its losses.

Jiang says present European leaders are American-controlled puppets who must be removed before peace is possible, and he predicts another five to ten years of warfare, a bloody Odessa phase, mass death, European revolution, and only then a ceasefire.

The host pivots from Ukraine to psychohistory as a governing technology and asks whether China might eventually apply AI and supervised machine learning on top of Jiang's framework to guide state decision-making.
Jiang says he hopes psychohistory-based AI governance becomes real, but paradigm inertia in academia makes it a century-scale project rather than an immediate policy program.
The host asks whether, despite cultural diversity and different national experiences, there are universal precepts that could ground human flourishing across boundaries.
Jiang answers that human flourishing has cross-cultural constants: love, learning, creativity, and socially productive contribution.
The host asks what can be done about elite overproduction and power illiteracy, treating them as barriers to a data-, imagination-, and love-guided society.

Jiang answers indirectly by diagnosing an approaching dark age driven by cascading systemic crises, predicting a civilizational reset, and expressing hope that whatever emerges afterward will use game theory and psychohistory to build a better society.
The host closes on guarded optimism, Jiang thanks him, and the program signs off.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang compresses his whole method into a psychological reading of states as if they were persons whose past behavior can be empathically modeled.
signature_moments.source_phrase: I see nation states as individuals
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's governing move: geopolitics becomes legible by importing person-level memory, motive, and empathy into state analysis.

signature_moments.moment: Elite rule appears here as a tragic cycle in which arrogance destroys the very society it tries to dominate, clearing the way for a replacement order.
signature_moments.source_phrase: because of their hubris, because of their arrogance, they will lead their societies to collapse
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It sets Jiang's cyclical theory of political succession and explains why he answers elite capture with long-duration historical turnover rather than immediate reform.

signature_moments.moment: History is recast from neutral scholarship into an ideological weapon wielded by victors.
signature_moments.source_phrase: history is not an objective study of the human condition. It's really a tool of indoctrination
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the interview's first sharp reversal: the standard archive of history is itself accused of being part of the problem Jiang is trying to solve.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang answers liberal triumphalism by calling neoliberalism not progress but a colonial extraction machine.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Neoliberalism is just a mechanism of colonial exploitation
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the packet its strongest polemical edge and anchors his refusal to treat post-Cold War Western ideology as historically vindicated.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns prediction into a courtroom for historical narratives: if a model cannot risk failure, it is still trapped in indoctrination.
signature_moments.source_phrase: forcing it to make predictions
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's central discipline principle, converting historical interpretation from rhetoric into something that can be tested against the future.

signature_moments.moment: Moral language is stripped of innocence and recast as an elite instrument for war and rule.
signature_moments.source_phrase: a way for the elite to enforce its war and power over people
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It sharpens the packet from abstract relativism into Jiang's stronger claim that value systems are often geopolitical weapons.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang answers the individualism-versus-collectivism dispute by insisting on a moving spectrum of human plurality rather than one correct civilizational formula.
signature_moments.source_phrase: recognize the diversity, the plurality, the openness and the dynamism of the human experience
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This gives the packet its most constructive social vision and prevents his anti-universalism from collapsing into nihilism.

signature_moments.moment: Game theory is accused of failure not because it is too strategic, but because it is not empathic enough to inhabit an opponent's rationality.
signature_moments.source_phrase: too mathematical and not psychological enough
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It links Jiang's method back to psychohistory and sets up his Ukraine reading as an empathy test rather than a mere geopolitical preference.

signature_moments.moment: The American order is condensed into a single imperial reflex: disagreement itself is treated as irrationality.
signature_moments.source_phrase: If you disagree, then you are irrational
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's cleanest statement of hegemony as epistemic domination, not just military or economic force.

signature_moments.moment: Trump is cast not as an anomaly but as a Caesar figure summoned by a decadent oligarchic republic that can no longer reconcile elites and people.
signature_moments.source_phrase: a false messiah of the Roman people
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns a contemporary election reading into Jiang's deeper cyclical model of republican breakdown, savior politics, and impending internal conflict.

signature_moments.moment: America's liberal mask is said to have dropped, revealing piracy and mafia-style coercion where a rules-based order once claimed legitimacy.
signature_moments.source_phrase: before America was very much protective of global naval trade, now America's behaving like pirates
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's sharpest reversal: imperial continuity remains, but the style changes from hypocrisy to open plunder.

signature_moments.moment: The global order is reduced to a pack hierarchy in which Europe kneels, Israel bites as a pit bull, and Putin survives by strategic flexibility.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Israel is the pit bull
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It compresses Jiang's view of allied behavior into vivid status roles instead of abstract alliance terminology.

signature_moments.moment: Retreat is denied; empire survives by making its vassals into cannon fodder and calling that strategic adjustment.
signature_moments.source_phrase: divide and rule
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives Jiang's answer to the interventionism question: less liberal rhetoric does not mean less empire, only a colder use of proxies.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang makes Iran the hinge on which control of Eurasia turns, arguing that Washington's deepest fear is not Tehran alone but a peaceful continental bloc that escapes American sea power.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the great fear of the American empire is an alliance between Russia, Iran, and China
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This condenses his larger imperial model: the United States attacks not only enemies but any infrastructure for a non-maritime Eurasian order.

signature_moments.moment: He reframes war aims from conquest to developmental mutilation: the point is to smash enough infrastructure that the target economy loses decades and regional integration becomes impossible.
signature_moments.source_phrase: destroy the Iranian infrastructure enough so that the economy is set back decades
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This gives a sharp Jiang distinction between winning a war and rendering a country unusable inside an alternative world system.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns an Iran strike into an imperial-suicide scenario: America goes in, overstretches, collapses, and leaves Israel holding the inheritance.
signature_moments.source_phrase: America will go into Iran, and America will overstretch itself, and America will collapse
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is a full causal chain rather than a single forecast, linking sabotage, imperial exhaustion, and regional succession.

signature_moments.moment: He refuses the live-war framing and says the decisive outcome is already in the past: the war was over a year ago even if the killing continues.
signature_moments.source_phrase: this war was over a year ago
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is Jiang's clearest compression of his Ukraine position in this packet: battlefield chronology and public chronology are not the same thing.

signature_moments.moment: The host turns Jiang's sunk-cost critique into a casino image and asks who will play the role of security escort when Ukraine's gamblers refuse to leave the table.
signature_moments.source_phrase: just like in a casino, the more you lose, the harder it is to stop betting
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It sharpens the packet's core question: if every elite layer profits from continuation, war termination cannot be explained by rational self-correction inside the existing system.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang strips away civilizational rhetoric and says the war is really a looting operation run through the Western military-industrial complex.
signature_moments.source_phrase: this war is really about stealing as much money as you can while this war is happening
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's sharpest reversal: instead of treating escalation as strategic error or idealist zeal, he reads it as profitable extraction by insulated elites.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang relocates the war's real theater from Ukraine itself to Europe by arguing that Odessa matters less as a Ukrainian city than as the place where European commitment gets exposed and broken.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it doesn't really matter what happens to Ukraine. It matters what happens in Europe
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's key model shift. It turns Ukraine into the trigger and Europe into the true decision-maker, which underwrites the later conscription and regime-change predictions.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang compresses his peace timeline into a brutal sequence: puppet leaders, five to ten more years, a bloody Odessa, revolution, then ceasefire.
signature_moments.source_phrase: this peace will have to be won on the battlefield
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The line preserves the packet's cold logic that peace does not come from diplomacy or exhaustion but from a prior internal political break inside Europe.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang frames psychohistory not as a forecast gimmick but as a century-scale blueprint for an AI advisor that can simulate many futures before leaders choose.
signature_moments.source_phrase: I'm not thinking about tomorrow. I'm thinking about, like, 100 years from now.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns his method from punditry into institutional design and makes clear that paradigm replacement, not short-term prediction, is the real ambition.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang compresses his universal ethics into three recurring human drives: love, creativity, and learning.
signature_moments.source_phrase: every human strives for love, for creativity, and for learning
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is his clearest positive definition in the interview of what flourishing would actually optimize for across cultures.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang answers elite overproduction by widening the aperture to a whole civilizational collapse, then flips that darkness into a resilience-and-rebirth image.
signature_moments.source_phrase: we are entering a world of darkness, we still will shine with great light at the end of it
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The closing image keeps the interview from ending in pure systems despair; it states his reset logic and his optimism in one memorable line.

Jiang's label for the present hegemonic order, defined by the universal imposition of American values and by treating disagreement as irrationality.
Jiang uses this for a populist savior figure like Caesar or Trump who appears to rescue the people while emerging from a decaying oligarchic order.
Invoked here as the imperial principle that the Western Hemisphere belongs to America and outside great powers should be excluded from South America.
